newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan ponders France nuclear fast-breeder bail-out.
newsitem.headline: Japan ponders France nuclear fast-breeder bail-out.

text.p: France's decision to abandon its multi-billion dollar fast-breeder nuclear reactor program has churned up fresh debate in Japan, where government officials have been unable to kick-start a similarly expensive initiative since its breakdown in December 1995.

In his first policy statement to France's National Assembly since his his election on June 1, Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday he would axe France's controversial $10.5 billion Superphenix nuclear fast-breeder.

Constructed 20 years ago with the alluring promise of a technology that could create more plutonium than it consumed, the 1,200 megawatt facility has provided just two and a half years of commercial value in its lifetime, making it one of the industry's most celebrated white elephants.
Similar references have been made to Japan's $6 billion "Monju" prototype fast-breeder reactor, which has never been a commercial asset and costs Japan some 20 billion yen ($175 million) annually.
But officials from Japan's Science and Technology Agency said France's decision will likely not alter the course of Japan's fast-breeder reactor program.
"This might be of some negative psychological impact but just because France is terminating the project does not mean Japan has to follow suit," said an agency official.

The 280,000 kilowatt Monju facility, designed to burn plutonium refined from the spent fuel of conventional reactors, was long thought to be the most promising panacea for a country forced to import nearly 100 percent of its oil and gas needs.
But an accident involving the leakage of liquid sodium from Monju's cooling system forced a manual shutdown of the plant in December 1995.
Dormant ever since, the plant has become emblematic of a growing identity crisis within Japan's ambitious but scandal-ridden campaign to make atomic energy the cornerstone of its power mix.
Critics of Monju took the French news as a positive sign.

"We welcome this very rational decision by the French government and feel it would be a very good time for Japan to reconsider Monju," said Jinzaburo Takagi, Executive Director of Japan's Citizens' Nuclear Information Center.
"France's FBR program had no commercial viability and was kept alive mainly for political or symbolic reasons. The same is true in Japan," he said.
